Cycling TODOs in a query buffer (from SPC r q t) is lossy. It can only go from pending to in progress, or from in progress to done. Then once it is done, it is removed from the preview. We should be able to arbitrarily cycle. The initial query should only show pending or in progress TODOs, but the ones that are cycled to done should not disappear unless the preview is refreshed.

Resolved. Full cycling (pending \to in-progress \to done \to cancelled \to pending) implemented via forester-cycle-todo-state. The query buffer forester-query-cycle-state updates status in-place so done items remain visible until manual refresh. Completion metadata is set/removed correctly when entering/leaving done state. The earlier replace-match backslash error was fixed by using literal mode.

Deprecated (2026-05-29). This investigation predates the Theme Studio redesign — most concrete claims here (single Dracula overlay, Inria Sans bundled fonts, \meta{layout}{wide} actually working) are no longer true. See Theme Studio — the current forest theme for the current architecture. Kept for historical context.

Investigation note: how much of the forest's look — fonts, layout, home page, color — can I customize without forking the compiler? Inspired by Matteo Capucci's forest, whose home page and overall typography depart noticeably from the default Forester theme.

The current theme is the upstream Forester base theme plus a few local additions — see theme/style.css (~830 lines), the Dracula theme overlay at theme/themes/dracula.css, the bundled Inria Sans @font-face declarations, and the dashboard's grid/column layout driven by \meta{layout}{wide}. The XSL pipeline (default.xsl → core.xsl, tree.xsl, links.xsl, metadata.xsl) is unchanged from upstream.
In rough order of cost to change, these are the levers Forester actually exposes.

Anything visual — fonts, colors, spacing, max-widths, column behavior, sticky sidebars, link styling, code block treatment — is a theme/style.css edit. A new theme like themes/dracula.css demonstrates the pattern: scope rules under a class injected by \meta{theme}{name} so multiple themes can coexist. Capucci's narrower main column, prominent serif body, and quiet metadata are almost certainly all CSS.

Add .woff2 files under theme/fonts/ and declare them via @font-face in style.css, then update the body font-family stack. Replacing Inria Sans with a serif (e.g. EB Garamond, Crimson Pro, Equity, Concourse) or a more distinctive sans (Inter Display, Fraunces) is a one-file edit. KaTeX fonts are independent and should be left alone.

\meta{layout}{wide|dashboard|table|kanban} and \meta{theme}{dracula|...} inject CSS classes (see the compiler's Htmx_client.ml) that you can target from style.css. New layouts cost nothing on the OCaml side — pick a name, add the class hook, write the CSS. The home page already exploits this with layout-wide.

The home page is just a tree (trees/public/index.tree) — its structure is fully under your control via \transclude, \grid/\col, and per-tree metadata. Capucci-style "front of forest" layouts (a short bio, a hand-curated featured-trees list, a recent-activity column) are achievable today by editing index.tree and writing a couple of CSS rules; no compiler change needed.

Structural changes — moving the TOC, suppressing metadata blocks, restructuring the article header, changing how transclusions are wrapped — live in theme/tree.xsl (~490 lines) and friends. Editable in-place, but easy to break, and changes drift from upstream on every theme/ submodule update. Reserve for things CSS genuinely cannot do.

Behavioral changes — collapsible sections, hover transclusions, search affordances — go here. Highest blast radius and least likely to survive an upstream update; consider only after CSS and XSL have been ruled out.

New CSS class injection points, new metadata-driven hooks, new built-in macros, new Datalog relations. Already on the table via the forkester effort; should remain a last resort for theming work specifically.

html:ul.html:li: Narrower body column with a serif. A 60–70ch max-width on the article column, paired with a serif body font, is the single biggest visual shift and is pure CSS.
Quieter metadata. Default Forester surfaces tree IDs, dates, taxons fairly prominently; Capucci tucks them away. .metadata { font-size: 0.85em; color: var(--muted) } territory.
Restructured home page. Replace the current bio + transclusion stack with a hand-curated front matter (recent writing, ongoing projects, a "what I'm reading" block) — pure index.tree edit.
Sectioned sidebar nav. A persistent left rail listing top-level topics. Achievable with a new \meta{layout}{...} that adds a sidebar slot, then CSS grid for placement.
Should new themes be shipped as switchable overlays (\meta{theme}{name}, like Dracula today) or as a single replaced base style? Overlays let you A/B variants per tree but balloon CSS quickly.
How much should diverge from the upstream base theme before maintenance pain (submodule conflicts on theme/) outweighs the visual gain? Vendoring theme/ fully is one answer.
Do any of the desired layout changes actually require XSL edits, or is CSS grid + class hooks sufficient? Worth prototyping the Capucci home-page rework in pure CSS first to find out.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pick one Capucci-inspired change — most likely the narrow-serif body — and prototype it as a new \meta{theme}{...} overlay so it can coexist with the current look. That single experiment will surface most of the customization-cost questions above without committing to a full redesign.

Investigation note on a narrow question: should there be tooling to convert Org, LaTeX, and Markdown into Forester .tree files? Export in the other direction, and full round-trip, are explicitly out of scope — see the Scope subtree below.

Two use cases dominate. First, migration: legacy Org Roam notes (see Forking Forester) and scattered LaTeX drafts should be ingestible without hand-translation. Second, collaboration: pulling in external Markdown or LaTeX material — a co-author's section, a paper appendix, a gist — and committing it as one or more trees.
Both cases are one-way lifts. Once content lands in a .tree, it is expected to be hand-edited toward Forester-native idioms (macros, transclusion, subtrees).
In scope: Org, LaTeX, Markdown → .tree. Via Pandoc is the obvious route since Pandoc already reads all three into a common AST.

Out of scope: Forester → anything else. Round-trip. Preserving lossless fidelity across multiple conversions. The forest graph (transclusion, Datalog, macros) is the hard part of Forester, and it is a write-only concern here.
Each takes Pandoc's universal reader set for free and differs in how it emits .tree markup.

Write a custom Pandoc writer in Lua that emits Forester markup directly. Invoked as pandoc -t forester.lua input.org -o sss-XXXX.tree. Lowest friction, no OCaml changes. Pandoc handles every input format automatically. Lua writers are well-documented and locally debuggable.

Shell out to pandoc with JSON output and consume the AST in a small OCaml (or Python) tool that emits .tree. Same upstream surface as the Lua writer, but the conversion logic lives in a language with real types. Worth it only if the Lua writer strains under macro-recognition rules.

Add Org/LaTeX/Markdown readers as siblings to the existing lib/parser/ menhir grammar, so forester build ingests them natively. Highest integration cost, reinvents Pandoc's readers, and couples this feature to the compiler. Rejected unless Pandoc turns out to be structurally unsuitable.
Tentative preference: start with the Lua writer. It is the smallest thing that could work and it contains the blast radius — a broken converter cannot break forester build.
Pandoc's AST has no notion of Forester macros, transclusion, Datalog, or the forest graph. Everything interesting gets decided on the way down. A deliberate policy is needed for:

html:ul.html:li: Headings → \subtree{\title{...}} vs. multiple top-level trees. A depth threshold (say, split at h1, subtree beneath) is probably right.
Math. Pandoc already represents math as LaTeX; #{...} and ##{...} fall out for free. But raw \mathbb{C} won't become \CC — macro recognition is a separate, opt-in pass.
Links. Intra-document anchors and external URLs both become [text](target), but cross-tree links need manual rewiring after import — Pandoc has no way to know which Org IDs map to which sss-XXXX.
Org metadata / YAML frontmatter. #+TITLE → \title, tags → \tag{...}, dates → \date{...}. Author defaults to stevenschaefer.
Code blocks, quotes, emphasis, lists. Mechanical.
Unknowns (raw HTML, unsupported inlines): preserve as \code{...} or a verbatim block rather than dropping.
Is macro recognition (recognizing \mathbb{C} and rewriting to \CC) a post-pass or built into the writer? Post-pass is simpler and lets the set of macros stay fluid.
Should the importer split one input file into many trees (one per top-level section, transcluded from a parent) or keep it as a single tree? Probably a CLI flag.
How are images and assets handled? Copy into assets/ and rewrite paths, or leave as-is and let the user move them?
Is there value in round-tripping Forester → Pandoc JSON just for testing (a sanity check that the evaluated AST survives a write-read cycle)? Probably not worth building yet.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Before committing to any of this as a forkester feature, try the Lua writer path on one real Org Roam note and one real LaTeX section. That prototype will make the lossy-boundary decisions concrete and clarify whether the Lua writer is adequate or whether the JSON-consumer route is needed.
Referenced from Rich Forest Rendering in Emacs. Shows concrete examples of Forester markup that renders well in a browser but degrades to plain text in the current Emacs preview.
Inline math. Source: #{e^{i \pi} + 1 = 0}. In-browser: e^{i \pi } + 1 = 0. In current Emacs preview: the raw source, with no KaTeX rendering.
Display math. Source: ##{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} = e}. In-browser:
In the current Emacs preview this shows up as one long line of TeX-looking source with no formatting.
Inline markup. \em{italic}, \strong{bold}, and \code{monospace} all have visual distinction in the browser but currently flatten to indistinguishable runs of characters in the text preview.

Transclusion. A \transclude{sss-XXXX} call in the browser expands the target tree inline, often with its own math, code, and links. In the Emacs preview it shows as a literal \transclude call — the reader has to navigate away to see the content.

Datalog queries. Source like the status-pending query in Features for Forking Forester produces a live list of trees in the browser but renders as a raw \query\datalog{...} block in Emacs with no results.
Links and cross-references. [title](sss-XXXX) is a clickable navigation in the browser; in the Emacs preview it's plain text with no indication that it's a link target.
